(p-٣٥٧) **Surat al-Ma'arij**

This surah is called *Sa'ala sa'il* (“A Questioner Asked”). It is also called *Surat al-Ma'arij* (The Ascending Stairways) and *Surat al-Waqi'* (The Event).

It is entirely Meccan, by the **consensus (ijma')** of scholars.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A questioner asked﴾. The commentators (*mufassirun*) said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. This is the view of the majority, including Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said it was Abu Jahl.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *sala* (p-٣٥٨) without a hamza. The rest read it with a hamza. Whoever reads *sa'ala* with a hamza has three opinions:

First: a caller called down upon himself a punishment that is certain to come.

Second: a questioner asked about a punishment that is certain to come: for whom is it, upon whom will it descend, and when will it occur? This is said in mockery, and the *ba'* (in *bi-'adhab*) then means "about" (*'an*). They recited as evidence:

*"If you ask me about women, I am well-informed about the ailments of women, a physician."*

Third: a questioner asked for a punishment that is certain to come, and the *ba'* is extra (*za'idah*).

Whoever reads without a hamza has two opinions:

One: it is also from *su'al* (asking), but the hamza was softened, so one says *sa'ala* and *sala*. Al-Farra' recited:

*"Come, let them ask, so that people may know which of us follows his companion at the beginning of time."*

Two: the meaning is that a valley (*wadi*) in Hell flowed with punishment for the disbelievers. This is the view of Zayd ibn Thabit, Zayd ibn Aslam and his son 'Abd al-Rahman. Ibn 'Abbas and others read *sala sayl* with a fatha on the *sin* and a sukun on the *ya'*, without an alif or hamza.

(p-٣٥٩) If we say it is from asking, then His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for the disbelievers﴾ is the answer to the question, as if, when he asked "For whom is this punishment?", it was said: "For the disbelievers." *Al-waqi'* means *al-ka'in* (that which exists). The meaning is that the punishment this disbeliever asked about is certainly going to befall the disbelievers in the Hereafter, ﴿there is no repeller of it from Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that this punishment comes from Allah upon the disbelievers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾. There are two views:

One: they are the heavens. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said they are the stairways of the angels. Ibn Qutaybah said: the origin of *al-ma'arij* is "steps," from *'araja*, meaning "he ascended." Al-Farra' said: since the angels ascend to Him, He described Himself thus. Al-Khattabi said: *al-ma'arij* are steps, singular *ma'raj*, which is a ladder, the means by which the deeds of the servants and the souls of the believers are ascended. So *al-ma'arij* are the paths along which one ascends.

Two: *al-ma'arij* are bounties and blessings. This was said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾. Al-Kisa'i read *ya'ruju* with a *ya'*.

Regarding "the Spirit" (*al-ruh*), there are two views:

One: Jibril (Gabriel), said by most scholars.

Two: the spirit of the dead person at the time it is taken, said by Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to Him﴾, meaning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿In a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾. There are two views:

One: it is the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Qurazi. This is the measure of the Day of Resurrection from the time of the raising up until the separation of the creation. (p-٣٦٠) It is reported in a hadith: "It will be made light for the believer until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." It was also said: Indeed, were anyone other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to take charge of the reckoning of creation, it would not be finished in fifty thousand years, whereas the Truth will finish it in an hour of a day. 'Ata' said: Allah will finish the reckoning of the creation within the measure of half a day of the days of this world. According to this, the meaning is: there is no repeller from Allah on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. It was also said the meaning is: a questioner asked about a punishment that is certain to come on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. According to this, there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence.

Two: the measure of the angels' ascent from the lowest part of the earth to the Throne, were anyone else to ascend it, would be fifty thousand years. This is the meaning of Mujahid's saying.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be patient﴾, i.e., be patient in the face of their denial of you, ﴿with gracious patience﴾, without complaint. This was before he was commanded to fight them, and then it was **abrogated (naskh)** by the verse of the sword. ﴿Indeed they see it as distant﴾, meaning the punishment is not certain to come, ﴿but We see it as near﴾, meaning certain to come, because everything that is coming is near.

Then He told when it will be, saying: ﴿On a Day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾, which we explained in [al-Kahf: 29]. ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool﴾, i.e., like wool. He likened them in their weakness and softness to wool. It was also said: He likened them to it in their lightness and their movement, because it has been reported that they will move as their forms, and they will be like dust. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'ihn* is wool, singular *'ihnah*, and it is said *'ihnah* and *'ihn* like *suf-ah* and *suf*. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-'ihn* is dyed wool.

(p-٣٦١) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾. Most readers read *yas'alu* with a fatha on the *ya'*. The meaning is: no close relative will ask about his relative, being preoccupied with himself. Muqatil said: a man will not ask about his relatives, nor speak to them, because of the intensity of the terrors. Mu'awiyah, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the *ya'*. The meaning is: it will not be said to the intimate friend: "Where is your friend?"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will be shown to them﴾, i.e., the intimate friend will be made known to his friend until he recognizes him, yet despite that he will not ask about his condition, nor speak to him, being preoccupied with himself. It is said: *baṣṣartu Zaydan kadha*, meaning: I made Zayd know such-and-such, if you inform him of it. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is: a relative will not ask about his relative, but they will be shown to them, i.e., they will be made known to them. Qatadah, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu 'Imran read *yubsiruna-hum* with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *sad*, with a kasra.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The guilty one would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾, i.e., the polytheist wishes that ransom would be accepted from him, ﴿and his spouse﴾, who is his wife, ﴿and his brother﴾, ﴿and his kin who sheltered him﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: *fasilatuhu* means his clan. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the nearest of his tribe to him. The meaning of *tu'wih* (sheltered) is that it gathers him, so he wishes to ransom himself with these mentioned persons, ﴿and then that it would deliver him﴾, that ransom would save him. ﴿No!﴾, that will not save him. ﴿Indeed, it is a blaze of Hellfire﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is one of the names of Hell, and therefore it is not declined. Others said: its meaning in the language is pure flame. Ibn al-Anbari said: it was named *Laza* because of the intensity of its blazing and flaming. It is said: he is *yatalaza*, meaning he flames and blazes. Thus fire is said to be *tatalaza*, intending this meaning. They recited:

*"A blazing hell that never abates for a moment, nor does its heat cool through the length of time."*

﴿Stripping away the scalp﴾. The majority read *nazza'atun lil-shawa* with a raised form, meaning: it is *nazza'ah*.

(p-٣٦٢) 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Abu Razin, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Hafs from 'Asim read *nazza'atan* in the accusative. Al-Zajjaj said: this is as a confirming circumstantial clause (*hal mu'akkidah*), as He said: ﴿It is the truth confirming﴾ [Fatir: 31]. It may also be accusative in the sense: "Indeed, it blazes, stripping away."

Regarding the meaning of *al-shawa*, there are four views:

One: the skin of the head. This was said by Mujahid.

Two: the fine features of the face. This was said by al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Three: the sinews and the heels. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

Four: the extremities: the two hands, the two feet, and the head. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It calls those who turned their backs﴾ on faith, ﴿and turned away﴾ from the truth. The commentators said: it says, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" ﴿And gathered and hoarded﴾. Al-Farra' said: meaning he gathered wealth into a container and did not pay its zakat from it, nor did he keep ties of kinship with it.

Al-Khattabi said: *al-ma'arij* are steps, singular *ma'raj*, which is a ladder, the means by which the deeds of the servants and the souls of the believers are ascended. So *al-ma'arij* are the paths along which one ascends.

Two: *al-ma'arij* are bounties and blessings. This was said by Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾. Al-Kisa'i read *ya'ruju* with a *ya'*.

Regarding "the Spirit" (*al-ruh*), there are two views:

One: Jibril (Gabriel), said by most scholars.

Two: the spirit of the dead person at the time it is taken, said by Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿to Him﴾, meaning to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿In a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years﴾. There are two views:

One: it is the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Qurazi. This is the measure of the Day of Resurrection from the time of the raising up until the separation of the creation. (p-٣٦٠) It is reported in a hadith: "It will be made light for the believer until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." It was also said: Indeed, were anyone other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to take charge of the reckoning of creation, it would not be finished in fifty thousand years, whereas the Truth will finish it in an hour of a day. 'Ata' said: Allah will finish the reckoning of the creation within the measure of half a day of the days of this world. According to this, the meaning is: there is no repeller from Allah on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. It was also said the meaning is: a questioner asked about a punishment that is certain to come on a Day whose measure is fifty thousand years. According to this, there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence.

Two: the measure of the angels' ascent from the lowest part of the earth to the Throne, were anyone else to ascend it, would be fifty thousand years. This is the meaning of Mujahid's saying.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be patient﴾, i.e., be patient in the face of their denial of you, ﴿with gracious patience﴾, without complaint. This was before he was commanded to fight them, and then it was **abrogated (naskh)** by the verse of the sword. ﴿Indeed they see it as distant﴾, meaning the punishment is not certain to come, ﴿but We see it as near﴾, meaning certain to come, because everything that is coming is near.

Then He told when it will be, saying: ﴿On a Day when the sky will be like molten brass﴾, which we explained in [al-Kahf: 29]. ﴿And the mountains will be like tufts of wool﴾, i.e., like wool. He likened them in their weakness and softness to wool. It was also said: He likened them to it in their lightness and their movement, because it has been reported that they will move as their forms, and they will be like dust. Al-Zajjaj said: *al-'ihn* is wool, singular *'ihnah*, and it is said *'ihnah* and *'ihn* like *suf-ah* and *suf*. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-'ihn* is dyed wool.

(p-٣٦١) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾. Most readers read *yas'alu* with a fatha on the *ya'*. The meaning is: no close relative will ask about his relative, being preoccupied with himself. Muqatil said: a man will not ask about his relatives, nor speak to them, because of the intensity of the terrors. Mu'awiyah, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Abu Ja'far read it with a damma on the *ya'*. The meaning is: it will not be said to the intimate friend: "Where is your friend?"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will be shown to them﴾, i.e., the intimate friend will be made known to his friend until he recognizes him, yet despite that he will not ask about his condition, nor speak to him, being preoccupied with himself. It is said: *baṣṣartu Zaydan kadha*, meaning: I made Zayd know such-and-such, if you inform him of it. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of the verse is: a relative will not ask about his relative, but they will be shown to them, i.e., they will be made known to them. Qatadah, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Abu 'Imran read *yubsiruna-hum* with a sukun on the *ba'* and a light *sad*, with a kasra.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The guilty one would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾, i.e., the polytheist wishes that ransom would be accepted from him, ﴿and his spouse﴾, who is his wife, ﴿and his brother﴾, ﴿and his kin who sheltered him﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: *fasilatuhu* means his clan. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the nearest of his tribe to him. The meaning of *tu'wih* (sheltered) is that it gathers him, so he wishes to ransom himself with these mentioned persons, ﴿and then that it would deliver him﴾, that ransom would save him. ﴿No!﴾, that will not save him. ﴿Indeed, it is a blaze of Hellfire﴾. Al-Farra' said: it is one of the names of Hell, and therefore it is not declined. Others said: its meaning in the language is pure flame. Ibn al-Anbari said: it was named *Laza* because of the intensity of its blazing and flaming. It is said: he is *yatalaza*, meaning he flames and blazes. Thus fire is said to be *tatalaza*, intending this meaning. They recited:

*"A blazing hell that never abates for a moment, nor does its heat cool through the length of time."*

﴿Stripping away the scalp﴾. The majority read *nazza'atun lil-shawa* with a raised form, meaning: it is *nazza'ah*.

It may also be accusative in the sense: "Indeed, it blazes, stripping away."

Regarding the meaning of *al-shawa*, there are four views:

One: the skin of the head. This was said by Mujahid.

Two: the fine features of the face. This was said by al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah.

Three: the sinews and the heels. This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

Four: the extremities: the two hands, the two feet, and the head. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It calls those who turned their backs﴾ on faith, ﴿and turned away﴾ from the truth. The commentators said: it says, "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" ﴿And gathered and hoarded﴾. Al-Farra' said: meaning he gathered wealth into a container and did not pay its zakat from it, nor did he keep ties of kinship with it.

This surah is called *Sa'ala sa'il* (“A Questioner Asked”). It is also called *Surat al-Ma'arij* (The Ascending Stairways) and *Surat al-Waqi'* (The Event).

It is entirely Meccan, by the **consensus (ijma')** of scholars.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A questioner asked﴾. The commentators (*mufassirun*) said: It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith when he said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. This is the view of the majority, including Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said it was Abu Jahl.

Abu Ja'far, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *sala* (p-٣٥٨) without a hamza. The rest read it with a hamza. Whoever reads *sa'ala* with a hamza has three opinions:

First: a caller called down upon himself a punishment that is certain to come.

Second: a questioner asked about a punishment that is certain to come: for whom is it, upon whom will it descend, and when will it occur? This is said in mockery, and the *ba'* (in *bi-'adhab*) then means "about" (*'an*). They recited as evidence:

*"If you ask me about women, I am well-informed about the ailments of women, a physician."*

Third: a questioner asked for a punishment that is certain to come, and the *ba'* is extra (*za'idah*).

One: it is also from *su'al* (asking), but the hamza was softened, so one says *sa'ala* and *sala*. Al-Farra' recited:

*"Come, let them ask, so that people may know which of us follows his companion at the beginning of time."*

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 70, verses 19–44:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious (haluʿan)﴾. Muqatil said: "He meant by it Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi." There are seven opinions concerning the word *halūʿ* (anxious, impatient).

The first is that it refers to the one described in the verses that follow this verse. This was narrated by ʿAṭiyyah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Zajjaj said the same.

The second is that it means one who is greedy for what is not lawful to him. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third is that it means stingy. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

The fourth is that it means miserly (*shaḥīḥ*). This was said by Ibn Jubayr.

The fifth is that it means excessively greedy (*sharih*). This was said by Mujahid.

The sixth is that it means fretful (*ḍajūr*). This was said by ʿIkrimah, Qatadah, Muqatil, and al-Farra'.

The seventh is that it means extremely impatient and distressed (*shadīd al-jazaʿ*). This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When evil touches him﴾, meaning: when poverty befalls him, ﴿he is distressed (jazūʿan)﴾, not patient and not seeking reward. ﴿And when good touches him﴾, meaning: when wealth befalls him, ﴿he is withholding (manūʿan)﴾, by withholding it from the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿Except for those who pray﴾, and they are the people of faith in Allah. He made the exception with the plural form from "mankind" because *insān* is a generic noun. ﴿Who are constant in their prayer﴾. Concerning them there are three opinions.

The first is that they are those who guard the obligatory prayers. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Masʿud.

The second is that they do not turn their heads to their right or left during prayer. This was said by ʿUqbah ibn ʿAmir, and al-Zajjaj chose it. He said: "Its derivation is from *dāʾim*, meaning still or stagnant," as in the hadith that "he forbade urinating in stagnant water" (p-364).

The third is that they are those who frequently perform voluntary acts of worship. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾. The explanation of this verse and the one after it has already been given in [Adh-Dhariyat: 19], and we clarified the meaning of "the Day of Judgment" in [al-Fatihah]. What follows this has been explained in [al-Mu'minun: 7–8], up to His saying: ﴿for their trusts﴾. Ibn Kathir alone recited: "li-amanatihim" (singular). ﴿And those who are upright in their testimonies﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited: "bi-shahadatihim" (singular), in the form of the singular noun. Hafs from ʿAsim recited: "bi-shahadatihim" (plural). ﴿Standing firm﴾, meaning they uphold the truth in them and do not conceal them.

﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, that they rush toward you (muhṭiʿīn)﴾. This was revealed concerning a group of disbelievers who sat around the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mocking the Qur'an and denying it. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Muhṭiʿ* means one who fixes his gaze upon something and does not turn away from it." They used to look at the Prophet ﷺ with a look of enmity. The disagreement over the phrase ﴿rushing (muhṭiʿīn)﴾ has already been mentioned in [Ibrahim: 43] and [al-Qamar: 8].

His saying: ﴿from the right and from the left, in groups (ʿizīn)﴾. Al-Farra' said: *ʿizīn* means circles, groups; its singular is *ʿizah*. They used to gather around the Prophet ﷺ and say: "If these people enter Paradise, as Muhammad ﷺ says, then we will surely enter it before them." Then Allah's saying was revealed: ﴿Does every one of them aspire to enter a Garden of Bliss?﴾ Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, Talhah ibn Musarrif, al-Aʿmash, and al-Mufaddal from ʿAsim recited "an yudkhala" with a fatha on the *yāʾ* and a damma on the *khāʾ* (i.e., the passive form). Abu ʿUbaydah said: *ʿizīn* is the plural of *ʿizah*, like *thubah* and *thubīn*, so they are groups in dispersed form (p-365).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Never!﴾, meaning: that will not be. ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One is that it means from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh. The meaning is: no one deserves Paradise by claiming nobility over others, since the origin is one, and one deserves it only through obedience.

The second is that it means: We created them from filth. So by what would they deserve Paradise when they have not believed? Bishr ibn Jihash narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that "he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾, then spat, and said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'How can you be beyond My power, when I created you from the likes of this? Until when I had perfected and balanced you, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth had a tread of you. Then you gathered and withheld, until when it reached the collarbones, you said: "Shall I give charity? When is the time for charity?"'" (p-366).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I swear by the Lords of the easts and the wests﴾. We have already spoken about this in [al-Haqqah: 38]. What is meant by "the easts and the wests" is the rising and setting of every day. ﴿Indeed, We are able to replace them with better than them﴾, meaning: We are able to create people better than them and more obedient to Allah when they disobey. ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾. This is explained in [al-Waqiʿah: 60]. ﴿So leave them to plunge in their falsehood﴾ and ﴿to amuse themselves﴾, meaning: to be heedless in their worldly life. ﴿Until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾. Ibn Muhaysin recited: "yalqaw yawmahumu alladhi yuʿadūn," and that is the Day of Resurrection. This is a command in form, but its meaning is a warning. The commentators mentioned that it is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse of the sword (*āyat al-sayf*). But if we say it is a warning of meeting the Day of Resurrection, then there is no basis for abrogation (*naskh*). ﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves rapidly﴾, meaning: they will come out quickly, as if they are racing.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿As if they were rushing to a target (nuṣub)﴾. Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs from ʿAsim recited with a damma on the *nūn* and the *ṣād*. Ibn Jarir said: it is the singular of *anṣāb*, which are their gods that they used to worship. So the meaning is: as if they were rushing toward their gods that they used to worship. Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited with a fatha on the *nūn* and a sukun on the *ṣād*. This is in the sense of the first recitation, except that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like the saying of the speaker: "I set up the thing (naṣabtu al-shay'a), I set it up (anṣibuhu) setting (naṣban)." Qatadah said: its meaning is: as if they were rushing toward a thing set up. Ibn Jarir said: its interpretation is: as if they were rushing toward an idol set up. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, and al-Nakhaʿi recited "nuṣbin" with a damma on the *nūn* and a sukun on the *ṣād* (p-367). Al-Hasan, Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi, and ʿAsim al-Jahdari recited "ila naṣabin" with a fatha on both the *nūn* and the *ṣād*. Ibn Qutaybah said: *nuṣub* is a stone that is set up or an idol; it is said *naṣb*, *nuṣb*, and *nuṣub*. Al-Farra' said: *naṣb* and *nuṣb* are the same, and it is a verbal noun, and its plural is *anṣāb*. Al-Zajjaj said: *naṣb* and *nuṣub* mean a raised marker. Al-Farra' said: *al-īfāḍ* means hastening.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and ʿAmr ibn Dinar recited "dhillatu dhālika al-yawm" without tanwin and with a *kasra* on the *mīm*. The rest of the surah has already been explained in [al-Maʿarij: 42].

Abu ʿUbaydah said: *ʿizīn* is the plural of *ʿizah*, like *thubah* and *thubīn*, so they are groups in dispersed form (p-365).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Never!﴾, meaning: that will not be. ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One is that it means from a drop of semen, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh. The meaning is: no one deserves Paradise by claiming nobility over others, since the origin is one, and one deserves it only through obedience.

The second is that it means: We created them from filth. So by what would they deserve Paradise when they have not believed? Bishr ibn Jihash narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that "he recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, We created them from what they know﴾, then spat, and said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'How can you be beyond My power, when I created you from the likes of this? Until when I had perfected and balanced you, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth had a tread of you. Then you gathered and withheld, until when it reached the collarbones, you said: "Shall I give charity? When is the time for charity?"'" (p-366).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I swear by the Lords of the easts and the wests﴾. We have already spoken about this in [al-Haqqah: 38]. What is meant by "the easts and the wests" is the rising and setting of every day. ﴿Indeed, We are able to replace them with better than them﴾, meaning: We are able to create people better than them and more obedient to Allah when they disobey. ﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾. This is explained in [al-Waqiʿah: 60]. ﴿So leave them to plunge in their falsehood﴾ and ﴿to amuse themselves﴾, meaning: to be heedless in their worldly life. ﴿Until they meet their Day which they are promised﴾. Ibn Muhaysin recited: "yalqaw yawmahumu alladhi yuʿadūn," and that is the Day of Resurrection. This is a command in form, but its meaning is a warning. The commentators mentioned that it is abrogated (*mansūkh*) by the verse of the sword (*āyat al-sayf*). But if we say it is a warning of meeting the Day of Resurrection, then there is no basis for abrogation (*naskh*). ﴿On the Day they emerge from the graves rapidly﴾, meaning: they will come out quickly, as if they are racing.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿As if they were rushing to a target (nuṣub)﴾. Ibn ʿAmir and Hafs from ʿAsim recited with a damma on the *nūn* and the *ṣād*. Ibn Jarir said: it is the singular of *anṣāb*, which are their gods that they used to worship. So the meaning is: as if they were rushing toward their gods that they used to worship. Ibn Kathir, ʿAsim, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited with a fatha on the *nūn* and a sukun on the *ṣād*. This is in the sense of the first recitation, except that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), like the saying of the speaker: "I set up the thing (naṣabtu al-shay'a), I set it up (anṣibuhu) setting (naṣban)." Qatadah said: its meaning is: as if they were rushing toward a thing set up. Ibn Jarir said: its interpretation is: as if they were rushing toward an idol set up. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Mijlaz, and al-Nakhaʿi recited "nuṣbin" with a damma on the *nūn* and a sukun on the *ṣād* (p-367). Al-Hasan, Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi, and ʿAsim al-Jahdari recited "ila naṣabin" with a fatha on both the *nūn* and the *ṣād*. Ibn Qutaybah said: *nuṣub* is a stone that is set up or an idol; it is said *naṣb*, *nuṣb*, and *nuṣub*. Al-Farra' said: *naṣb* and *nuṣb* are the same, and it is a verbal noun, and its plural is *anṣāb*. Al-Zajjaj said: *naṣb* and *nuṣub* mean a raised marker. Al-Farra' said: *al-īfāḍ* means hastening.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Humiliation will cover them﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and ʿAmr ibn Dinar recited "dhillatu dhālika al-yawm" without tanwin and with a *kasra* on the *mīm*. The rest of the surah has already been explained in [al-Maʿarij: 42].
